questions.q: What approaches have researchers used to reduce hallucinations in language models?
questions.summary: Researchers have employed various methods to reduce hallucinations in language models, including Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) [P1], which decreases hallucinations on list-based questions, and DoLa [P8], which improved truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12 to 17 absolute percentage points. These findings suggest that active validation and contrasting layers can effectively mitigate hallucinations.

findings_detail.finding: CoVe decreased hallucinations on list-based questions from Wikidata, closed-book MultiSpanQA, and long-form biography generation.
DoLa improved LLaMA models' truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12 to 17 absolute percentage points without retrieved knowledge or additional fine-tuning.

questions.q: How do you measure factual precision in long-form generation?
questions.summary: Factual precision in long-form generation is measured by breaking the text into atomic facts and evaluating the percentage of these facts supported by reliable knowledge sources, as seen in the FActScore method [P1]. This approach provides a finer-grained measure than simply judging the entire output as true or false.

findings_detail.finding: FActScore evaluates factual precision by breaking long-form text into atomic facts and measuring the percentage of these facts supported by reliable knowledge sources.

draft_findings_detail.finding: FActScore evaluates factual precision by breaking long-form text into atomic facts and measuring the percentage of these facts supported by reliable knowledge sources.

Human evaluation involves experts rating the factual accuracy of the generated content.
claims_detail.evidence: An automated estimator that uses retrieval and a strong language model approximates human FActScore with an error rate below 2%, which makes large-scale factuality evaluation practical.

questions.q: What benchmarks evaluate truthfulness of language models?
